video.title: How many different magic squares can one to nine make?
video.description: The magic square 8, 1, 6 / 3, 5, 7 / 4, 9, 2 can be turned and flipped. Turning and flipping it shows every magic square with one to nine, and counting the choices for one, six and eight proves there are no others.

in a magic square of 1 to 9 the centre must be 5; 1 and 9 cannot sit in corners, so they sit in the middles of edges, exactly opposite each other across the 5
choices: 1 can sit in the middle of any of the 4 edges; 9 then has no choice (opposite 1)
beside 1 on its edge go 6 and 8 (the only pair from what is left that adds to 15 - 1 = 14), in 2 possible orders
after that everything is forced: the two numbers beside 9 add to 6, so they are 2 and 4; 2 sits opposite 8 (8 + 5 + 2 = 15) and 4 opposite 6 (6 + 5 + 4 = 15); the last two boxes take 3 and 7
the 8 squares are the square turned 0, 1, 2, 3 quarter turns (4 squares), and each of those flipped like a mirror (4 more)
the slipped count of 4 counts only the turns
the book's answer key says there is exactly one magic square if rotations and reflections are ignored; the plan says 8 counting them; both are the same fact, and the video says both

video.title: What else can you do to a magic square and keep it magic?
video.description: The magic square 8, 1, 6 / 3, 5, 7 / 4, 9, 2 fills a board of nine boxes. Multiplying every number by itself makes the lines stop matching; taking away one from every number, multiplying by ten, dividing, and turning or flipping the square all keep it magic.
video.anchor: Which changes keep a magic square magic?
maths_rules: the starting square is 8, 1, 6 / 3, 5, 7 / 4, 9, 2; every row, column and diagonal adds to 15 (8+1+6, 3+5+7, 4+9+2, 8+3+4, 1+5+9, 6+7+2, 8+5+2, 6+5+4 all = 15)
the board has 9 boxes in 3 rows of 3; each box holds a number of the square; each line of three boxes adds to 15
adding 1 to every cell adds 3 to every line (15 to 18); doubling every cell doubles every line (15 to 30)
the slip squares every cell: 64, 1, 36 / 9, 25, 49 / 16, 81, 4; top row 64 + 1 + 36 = 101; middle row 9 + 25 + 49 = 83; 101 is not 83, so it is not magic

subtract 1 from every cell: 7, 0, 5 / 2, 4, 6 / 3, 8, 1; rows 7+0+5 = 12, 2+4+6 = 12, 3+8+1 = 12; columns 7+2+3 = 12, 0+4+8 = 12, 5+6+1 = 12; diagonals 7+4+1 = 12, 5+4+3 = 12; each line loses 3, 15 - 3 = 12; the box that held 1 now holds 0
divide every cell of the times-ten square by 5: 16, 2, 12 / 6, 10, 14 / 8, 18, 4; every line 150 / 5 = 30 (16+2+12 = 30); dividing needs a number that is not 0

turn the board a quarter turn clockwise: 4, 3, 8 / 9, 5, 1 / 2, 7, 6; rows 4+3+8, 9+5+1, 2+7+6 all 15; the old rows are now columns, and the diagonals stay diagonals; a mirror flip also keeps the same lines
answer (plan): subtract the same number from every cell, multiply or divide every cell by the same non-zero number, rotate or reflect the square; adding the same number keeps a square magic too

final_answer.value: subtract the same number from every cell, multiply or divide every cell by the same non-zero number, rotate or reflect the square
final_answer.spoken: take away the same number from every cell, multiply or divide every cell by the same number that is not zero, or turn or flip the square
